As a result, we have proved that for the upper-left sub-blocks:

$$ \lim_{t_{0}\to\infty}(\Sigma_{A})_{[t+1],[t+1]}=(\Sigma_{B})_{[t+1],[t+1]}. $$

For the rest of the elements in $\Sigma_{A}$ , note that the columns of $[Z_{e}^{t+t_{0}}|Z_{e}^{t+t_{0}-1}|\cdots|Z_{e}^{t_{0}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times(t+1)}$ becomes perfectly correlated as $t_{0}\to\infty$ , so those elements also converge to the corresponding elements in $\Sigma_{B}$

Thus we have shown $\lim_{t_{0}}\lVert\Sigma_{A}-\Sigma_{B}\rVert_{2}=0$ . From here, following the same argument as Equation (156)-(166) of the proof of Lemma 10, Berthier et al. [41], we arrive at

$$ \lvert\mathbb{E}[A]-\mathbb{E}[B]\rvert^{2}\leq\mathit{Constant}\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\Sigma_{A}+\Sigma_{B}-2(\Sigma_{B}^{1/2}\Sigma_{A}\Sigma_{B}^{1/2})^{1/2})=o(\lVert\Sigma_{A}-\Sigma_{B}\rVert_{2}), $$

where the $\mathit{Constant}$ does not depend on $p,t_{0},\Sigma_{A},\Sigma_{B}$ . This completes the proof of Lemma E.10. ∎

Now we are ready to show Lemma E.3.

#### Proof of Lemma E.3.

We first prove by induction on $t$ that $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , $\exists\,T_{0}$ s.t. $\forall\,t_{0}\geq T_{0}$ ,

$$ \lim_{p}\mathbb{P}\left[\frac{1}{p}\lVert v_{\textup{II}}^{t}-v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\epsilon\right]=1. $$

When $t=0$ , $v_{\textup{II}}^{0}=\zeta^{*}\cdot\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*}v_{1}^{t_{0}}/\tau_{1}^{*}+\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}\cdot\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*}Z_{\textup{II}}^{\mathrm{init}}$ , $v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{0}=\zeta^{*}\cdot\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*}v_{1}^{\infty}/\tau_{1}^{*}+\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}\cdot\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*}Z_{\textup{II}}^{\mathrm{init}}$ . Then Equation (E-34) directly follows from Lemma E.9. Now suppose we have proved Equation (E-34) for all $0\leq i\leq t-1$ . For $t$ ,

$$ \displaystyle v_{\textup{II}}^{t}= \displaystyle{\displaystyle X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-r_{\textup{II}}^{t-1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r_{1}^{t+t_{0}-1}))-(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\beta_{1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}^{(p)}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\eta^{t+t_{0}-1} \displaystyle+\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi(v_{\textup{II}}^{t-1},\eta^{t+t_{0}-1}), \displaystyle v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}= \displaystyle{\displaystyle X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-r_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r_{1}^{\infty}))-(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\beta_{1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}^{(p)}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}} \displaystyle+\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi(v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1},\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}), $$

and Equation (E-34) follows from Lemma E.9 and the induction hypothesis.

We know from Lemma E.2 that

$$ \displaystyle\phi\left(v_{\textup{II}}^{t},v_{\textup{II}}^{t-1},\cdots,v_{\textup{II}}^{1},v_{\textup{II}}^{0},v_{1}^{t+t_{0}},\eta^{t+t_{0}},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(Z_{\textup{II}}^{t},Z_{\textup{II}}^{t-1},\cdots,Z_{\textup{II}}^{1},Z_{\textup{II}}^{0},Z^{t+t_{0}}_{1},\eta(Z_{1}^{t+t_{0}},\cdots,Z_{E}^{t+t_{0}}),\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)\right]. $$

We wish to take $t_{0}\to\infty$ on both sides of Equation (E-35) to prove Lemma E.3.

For the LHS of Equation (E-35), by Equation (E-34) and Lemma E.9, $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , $\exists\,T_{0}$ s.t. $\forall\,t_{0}\geq T_{0}$ and $t\in\mathbb{N_{+}}$ ,

$$ \lim_{p}\mathbb{P}\left[\left\lvert\phi\left(v_{\textup{II}}^{t},\cdots,v_{\textup{II}}^{0},v_{1}^{t+t_{0}},\eta^{t+t_{0}},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)-\phi\left(v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t},\cdots,v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{0},v_{1}^{\infty},\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)\right\rvert\leq\epsilon\right]=1, $$

where the Gaussian variables are as they are defined in Lemma E.2.

For the RHS of Equation (E-35), by Lemma E.10, $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , $\exists\,T_{0}$ s.t. $\forall\,t_{0}\geq T_{0}$ and $t\in\mathbb{N_{+}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{p}\Big|\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(Z_{\textup{II}}^{t},Z_{\textup{II}}^{t-1},\cdots,Z_{\textup{II}}^{1},Z_{\textup{II}}^{0},Z^{t+t_{0}}_{1},\eta(Z_{1}^{t+t_{0}},\cdots,Z_{1}^{t+t_{0}}),\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)\right] \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t},Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1},\cdots,Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{1},Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{0},Z_{1},\overline{\eta},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)\right]\Big|<\epsilon, $$

where the Gaussian variables are as they are defined in the term ‘ $B$ ’ in Lemma E.10.

Putting the analysis of both sides together, we know

$$ \displaystyle\phi\left(v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t},v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1},\cdots,v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{1},v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{0},v_{1}^{\infty},\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t},Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1},\cdots,Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{1},Z_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{0},Z_{1},\overline{\eta},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\cdots,\beta_{E}\right)\right], $$

which completes the proof of Lemma E.3. ∎

#### E.1.4 Proof of Lemma E.4

Let $\widetilde{H}_{\textup{II}}(\cdot)=(H_{\textup{II}}(\cdot)-(\zeta^{*})^{2})/(1-(\zeta^{*})^{2})$ . By Lemma E.8, $\widetilde{H}_{\textup{II}}(\cdot)$ is increasing, strictly convex, $\widetilde{H}_{\textup{II}}(1)=1$ , $\widetilde{H}_{\textup{II}}(0)\geq 0$ . Also, $0\leq\frac{\mathrm{d}\widetilde{H}_{\textup{II}}(\rho)}{\mathrm{d}\rho}\leq\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}<1$ by the last equation in Assumption 8 (a). By Definition E.3,

$$ \lvert 1-\rho^{i,j}_{\textup{II}}\rvert\leq(\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}})\lvert 1-\rho^{i-1,j-1}_{\textup{II}}\rvert\leq(\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}})^{i}. $$

Thus $\limsup_{T\to\infty}\sup_{T\leq i<j}\lvert 1-\rho_{\textup{II}}^{i,j}\rvert=0$ . Also, $\mathop{\mathrm{plim}}_{p}\frac{1}{p}\lVert v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{i}-v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{j}\rVert_{2}^{2}=2(\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*})^{2}(1-\rho^{i,j}_{\textup{II}})$ , and $\xi^{t}=\eta(v^{t}_{{\textup{II},\infty}},\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})$ is Lipschitz in $v^{t}_{{\textup{II},\infty}}$ . Thus we have shown Lemma E.4.

#### E.1.5 Proof of Lemma E.5

Either $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{joint}}$ or $\mu_{\mathrm{ada}}$ , we can use the definition of $\xi$ in Eqn (20) to write out the KKT condition of $\xi^{t}=\xi(v_{\textup{II}}^{t},\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})$ ,

$$ \Sigma_{1}(\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})-\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}-(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}(\beta_{1}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})+\theta_{\textup{II}}^{*}\nabla\mu_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t};\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})\ni 0. $$

Set the LHS to exactly zero, and let $s^{t}_{\textup{II}}$ be the member of sub-gradient that solves the equation. Then we get

$$ s_{\textup{II}}^{t}=\frac{1}{\theta_{\textup{II}}^{*}}\left[\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}+(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}(\beta_{1}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})-\Sigma_{1}(\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})\right]\in\nabla\mu_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t};\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}). $$

To show the claim about $\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t})$ , we again use the $o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ notation defined in the proof of Lemma C.4 in Section C.1.4. To recall its definition, some sequence $X^{(p),t}=o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ iff $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , $\exists\,T$ s.t. $\forall\,t\geq T$ , $\lim_{p}\mathbb{P}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\lVert X^{{(p),t}}\rVert_{2}<\epsilon\right]=1$ .

By Lemma E.4, $v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t+1}-v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}=o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ , $\xi^{t+1}-\xi^{t}=o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ . From how the induced AMP iterates are defined in Definition E.2, we know

$$ \displaystyle y_{1}-r_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r^{\infty}_{1})=y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t}+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}^{(p)}(y_{1}-r_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r_{1}^{\infty})) \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle{\displaystyle X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}\left[y_{1}-r_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r^{\infty}_{1})\right] \displaystyle={X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{II}}{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}\left[y_{1}-r_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t-1}-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}(y_{1}-r_{1}^{\infty})\right] \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t+1}+(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\beta_{1}+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}^{(p)}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}-\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t}+o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p}) \displaystyle={X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{II}}\left[v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}+(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}^{(p)}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\beta_{1}+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}^{(p)}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}-\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t-1}\right] \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle v_{{\textup{II},\infty}}^{t}+(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\beta_{1}+\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}-\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t}=\frac{{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})}{1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}}+o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p}), $$

where the first equation is true just by plugging in the definition of $r^{t}_{{\textup{II},\infty}}$ , the second multiplies both sides with ${X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}$ , and the third equation has suppressed $(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}}^{(p)}-\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\cdot\kappa_{1}{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}(y_{1}-r^{\infty}_{1})$ into $o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ .

Compare the LHS of the last equation above to the definition of $s^{t}_{\textup{II}}$ , and recall that $\theta^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}})=1$ from Assumption 8 (a). We notice that

$$ s^{t}_{\textup{II}}=\frac{1}{\theta^{*}_{\textup{II}}}\cdot\frac{\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})}{1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}}+o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})=\Sigma_{1}{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})+o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p}). $$

Hence $\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t})=-\Sigma_{1}{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}^{{\top}}(y_{1}-{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\xi^{t})+s^{t}_{\textup{II}}+o^{*}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{p})$ . This concludes the proof of Lemma E.5.

#### E.1.6 Proof of Lemma E.6

The proof of Lemma E.6 only slightly differs for $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{joint}}$ and $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{ada}}$ . We will use the former as an example and the latter can be proved in an analogous way.

We define some re-scaled quantities for the subsequent proof. Let $\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}=\Sigma_{1}/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{1})$ , $\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}=\theta^{*}_{\textup{II}}/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{1})$ , $\widetilde{\tau}^{*}_{\textup{II}}=\tau^{*}_{\textup{II}}/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{1})}$ .

We consider $\overline{\xi}$ defined in Eqn (20) from Assumption 8 (a): $\overline{\xi}=\xi(\tau_{\textup{II}}^{*}(\zeta^{*}Z_{1}/\tau_{1}^{*}+\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}Z_{1}^{\prime}),\overline{\eta})$ , $\overline{\eta}=\eta(Z_{1},\cdots,Z_{E})$ where $Z_{1}^{\prime},(Z_{1}/\tau_{1}^{*}),(Z_{2}/\tau_{2}^{*}),\cdots,(Z_{E}/\tau_{E}^{*})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}N(0,I_{p})$ . We will be using the same set of Gaussian variables throughout the proof. We define an idealized version of $s_{\textup{II}}^{t}$ called $\overline{s}_{\textup{II}}$ ,

$$ \overline{s}_{\textup{II}}=\frac{1}{\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}}\left[\widetilde{\tau}_{\textup{II}}^{*}\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}(\zeta^{*}Z_{1}/\tau_{1}^{*}+\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}Z_{1}^{\prime})+(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}(\beta_{1}-\overline{\eta})-\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}(\overline{\xi}-\overline{\eta})\right]. $$

Then $\overline{s}_{\textup{II}}\in\nabla\mu_{\textup{II}}(\overline{\xi};\overline{\eta})$ , or in the case of the joint estimator, $\overline{s}_{\textup{II}}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}\in\partial\lVert\overline{\xi}-\overline{\eta}\rVert_{1}$ .

Define $\widetilde{\xi}^{t}=\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}+\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}s^{t}_{\textup{II}}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}$ . Recall we have defined $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(s^{t}_{\textup{II}})_{j}\rvert\geq\lambda_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ . Since $s^{t}_{\textup{II}}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}\in\partial\lVert\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}}\rVert_{1}$ , $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)$ can be equivalently written as $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(\widetilde{\xi}^{t})_{j}\rvert\geq\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ .

Define the idealized counterpart of $\widetilde{\xi}^{t}$ as $\bar{\tilde{\xi}}=\overline{\xi}-\overline{\eta}+\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}\overline{s}_{\textup{II}}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}$ . If we define the idealized counterpart of $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)$ as $\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(\overline{s}_{\textup{II}})_{j}\rvert\geq\lambda_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ , then the set $\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)$ also admits an equivalent form using $\bar{\tilde{\xi}}$ : $\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\geq\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ . We rearrange the terms of $\bar{\tilde{\xi}}$ to get an equivalent form:

$$ \bar{\tilde{\xi}}=(1-\kappa_{1}\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{I}})\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}(\beta_{1}-\overline{\eta})+\widetilde{\tau}^{*}_{\textup{II}}\zeta^{*}\widetilde{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}Z_{1}+\widetilde{\Sigma}^{1/2}_{1}\left[\widetilde{\tau}^{*}_{\textup{II}}\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}Z_{1}^{\prime}-(I_{p}-\widetilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{1})\widetilde{\Sigma}^{1/2}_{1}(\overline{\xi}-\overline{\eta})\right]. $$

The rest of the proof follows the same steps as those of Lemma C.5’s proof. For any $j\in[p]$ , use $\widetilde{\sigma}_{1,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ to denote the $j$ -th row of $\widetilde{\Sigma}^{1/2}_{1}$ but written as a vertical vector. By the normlization, we know $\lVert\widetilde{\sigma}_{1,j}\rVert_{2}\geq 1$ . Define $Z^{\prime}_{1,j}=\widetilde{\tau}^{*}_{\textup{II}}\sqrt{1-(\zeta^{*})^{2}}(\widetilde{\sigma}_{1,j})^{{\top}}Z^{\prime}_{1}$ . We write $(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}=h_{\textup{II},j}(Z^{\prime}_{1,j})$ , where $h_{\textup{II},j}(\cdot)$ also implicitly depends on $Z_{1},\cdots,Z_{E}$ and $P_{1,j}^{\bot}Z_{1}^{\prime}$ , $P_{1,j}^{\bot}$ being the projection matrix onto the orthogonal complement of $\Span(\widetilde{\sigma}_{1,j})$ . Note that these other Gaussian variables $h_{\textup{II},j}(\cdot)$ implicitly depends on are all independent of $Z_{1,j}^{\prime}$ ; conditioning on any values of those Gaussian variables, we have

$$ \lvert h_{\textup{II},j}(x_{1})-h_{\textup{II},j}(x_{2})\rvert\geq\frac{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{1})}{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_{1})}\lvert x_{1}-x_{2}\rvert $$

in the same way we have got Equation (C-20). We have omitted some details because they are analogous to the corresponding steps in the proof of Lemma C.5.

Note that $h_{\textup{II},j}(\cdot)$ is also Lipschitz in its argument. Similarly to Lemma C.8 used in the proof of Lemma C.5, we have the following fact written as a lemma:

#### Lemma E.11.

Let $\{I_{a}:a>0\}$ be a collection of intervals indexed by $a>0$ , satisfying $\lim_{a\downarrow 0}m(I_{a})=0$ where $m(\cdot)$ is the Lebesgue measure. Then $\lim_{a\downarrow 0}\sup_{p}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbf{1}{\{(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\in I_{a}\}}\right]=0$ .

We need yet Lemma E.12 before the proof of Lemma E.6 itself. It is analogous to Lemma C.9 for the proof of Lemma C.5.

#### Lemma E.12.

For any $t\in\mathbb{N_{+}}$ , any $c\in(0,1)$ , $\lvert S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)\rvert/p=\mathbb{E}[\lvert\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)\rvert/p]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1)$ .

#### Proof of Lemma E.12.

We fix $c$ for the rest of the proof. We define the notation $(x)_{+}=\max\{x,0\},\forall\,x\in\mathbb{R}$ . For $0<a<\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-c)/3$ , define a Lipschitz function $\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},1}(x):\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ : $\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},1}(x)=[1-(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-\lvert x\rvert)_{+}/a]_{+}$ . Then $\lvert\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},1}(x)-\vec{1}\{\lvert x\rvert\geq\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)\}\rvert\leq\vec{1}\{\lvert x\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c))\}$ .

For any $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , define $\mathrm{dist}(x)$ as the distance of $\lvert x\rvert$ to the interval $(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c))$ , i.e. $\mathrm{dist}(x)=(\lvert x\rvert-\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c))_{+}+(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-a-\lvert x\rvert)_{+}$ . Define another Lipschitz function $\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},2}(x):\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ : $\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},2}(x)=(1-\mathrm{dist}(x)/a)_{+}$ . Then $\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert x\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c))\}}\leq\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},2}(x)\leq\vec{1}\{\lvert x\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-2a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)+a)\}$ . For $i=1,2$ , define $\phi_{\textup{II},i}^{{(p)}}:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}$ : $\forall\,x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ , $\phi_{\textup{II},i}^{{(p)}}(x)=\sum_{j\in[p]}\phi^{(1)}_{\textup{II},i}(x_{j})$ . By Lemma F.1, both $\{\phi_{\textup{II},1}^{{(p)}}:p\geq 1\}$ and $\{\phi_{\textup{II},2}^{{(p)}}:p\geq 1\}$ are uniformly Lipschitz functions.

It is already known that $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(\widetilde{\xi}^{t})_{j}\rvert\geq\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ , $\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)=\{j\in[p]:\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\geq\widetilde{\theta}^{*}_{\textup{II}}(1-c)\}$ . By Lemma E.3, for any already chosen and fixed $a$ , as $p\to\infty$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert{\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c)\rvert}/{p}-\mathbb{E}[{\lvert\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)\rvert}/{p}]\right\rvert\leq \displaystyle\lvert\phi_{\textup{II},1}^{(p)}(\widetilde{\xi}^{t})-\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\textup{II},1}^{(p)}(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})]\rvert+\phi_{\textup{II},2}^{(p)}(\widetilde{\xi}^{t})+\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\textup{II},2}^{(p)}(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})]\leq 2\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\textup{II},2}^{(p)}(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{2}{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-2a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)+a)\}}]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1). $$

By Lemma E.11, for any $\epsilon>0$ , we can fix a small $a$ s.t.

$$ \sup_{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)-2a,\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c)+a)\}}]/p<\epsilon/4 $$

before taking $p\to\infty$ . Thus Lemma E.12 is proved. ∎

Finally we are ready to prove Lemma E.6.

#### Proof of Lemma E.6.

For any chosen and fixed $c\in(0,1)$ , by Lemma E.12, $\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c)\rvert/p=\mathbb{E}[\lvert\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)\rvert/p]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1)$ as $p\to\infty$ . Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\lvert\overline{S}_{\textup{II}}(c)\rvert/p]= \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert>\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}\}}\right]+\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}(1-c),\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}]\}}\right]. $$

By Lemma E.11, $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , $\exists\,c\in(0,1)$ close enough to 0, s.t. $\sup_{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert\in(\widetilde{\theta}^{*}(1-c),\widetilde{\theta}^{*}]\}}]/p<\epsilon$ . By the definition of $\bar{\tilde{\xi}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j\in[p]}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}{\{\lvert(\bar{\tilde{\xi}})_{j}\rvert>\widetilde{\theta}_{\textup{II}}^{*}\}}\right]= \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert\overline{\xi}-\overline{\eta}\rVert_{0}\right]=\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}^{(p)}\to\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}, $$

where the second equality is by Eqn (B-8) and the convergence is by Proposition 3.

By the choice of $c$ so far, we know it only depends on the ‘idealized’ quantities such as $\overline{\eta}$ and $\bar{\tilde{\xi}}$ , not any specific time step $t$ . As a result, $\forall\,\epsilon>0$ , there exists $c=c(\epsilon)\in(0,1)$ s.t. fixing any $c^{\prime}\in(0,c(\epsilon)]$ and any $t\in\mathbb{N_{+}}$ , we have $\lim_{p}\mathbb{P}\left[\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c^{\prime})\rvert/p\leq\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+\epsilon\right]=1$ . This completes the proof. ∎

#### E.1.7 Proof of Lemma E.7

The proof of Lemma E.7 is analogous to that of Lemma C.6 in Section C.1.6, so we may skip certain details. Just like Lemma E.6, the proof for the joint estimator ( $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{joint}}$ ) is only slightly different to the case of the adaptively weighted estimator ( $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{ada}}$ ). We do the former proof and the latter can be derived in an analogous way.

Recall how we have defined the sparse singular eigenvalues of a matrix in Section C.1.6: For any matrix $X$ having $p$ columns, any subset $S\subset[p]$ , define $\kappa_{-}(X,S)=\inf\left\{\lVert Xu\rVert_{2}:\mathrm{supp}(u)\subset S,\lVert u\rVert_{2}=1\right\}$ and the $k$ -sparse singular value

$$ \kappa_{-}(X,k)=\min_{S\subset[p],\lvert S\rvert\leq k}\kappa_{-}(X,S)=\min_{S\subset[p],\lvert S\rvert=k}\kappa_{-}(X,S). $$

#### Lemma E.13 (Lower Bound on the Sparse Singular Values).

Under Assumption 2, there exists small enough constants $\epsilon_{0}>0$ and $c_{0}>0$ , s.t. $\kappa_{1}\cdot(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+\epsilon_{0})<1$ , and $\forall\,\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0})$ ,

$$ \lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left[\kappa_{-}\left({X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2},p(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+\epsilon)\right)>c_{0}\right]=1. $$

The proof of Lemma E.13 is analogous to Lemma C.10 so it is omitted here.

#### Proof of Lemma E.7.

Define $\Delta\xi^{t}=\hat{\beta}_{\textup{II}}-\xi^{t}$ , where $\hat{\beta}_{\textup{II}}$ is the minimizer of $L_{\textup{II}}(\cdot)$ defined in Eqn (17). $L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t}+\Delta\xi^{t})\leq L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t})$ . Applying Lemma F.6(b) and then Lemma F.4(a) to ${X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}$ , we know $\sigma_{\max}({X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2})\leq 2(c_{1}/\kappa_{1})^{1/2}(1+\sqrt{\kappa_{1}})$ almost surely as $p\to\infty$ , in which $c_{1}$ is the constant from Assumption 2.

We now define the high-probability event we will be working on throughout the proof. We choose $M>1$ large enough and $\epsilon_{0}\in(0,1)$ small enough such that $\kappa_{1}\,(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+2{\epsilon_{0}})<1$ to satisfy the requirement of Lemma E.13 s.t. $\forall\,\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0})$ , $\exists\,T$ s.t. $\forall\,t\geq T$ , at the time step $t$ , the following conditions are satisfied simultaneously with probability going to 1 as $p\to\infty$ :

- (i) $\max\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\lVert\hat{\beta}_{\textup{II}}\rVert_{2},\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\lVert\xi^{t}\rVert_{2}\}\leq M$ (by Lemma E.1 and Lemma E.3);

- (ii) $\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\rvert\leq p(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+{\epsilon})$ for some $c_{2}=c_{2}(\epsilon)\in(0,1)$ (by Lemma E.6 with $c_{2}$ depending only on the specific $\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0})$ but invariant to the choice of the time step $t\in\mathbb{N_{+}}$ );

- (iii) $\kappa_{-}({X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2},p(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+2{\epsilon}))>c_{3}$ for some $c_{3}=c_{3}(\epsilon_{0})\in(0,1)$ (by Lemma E.13 with $c_{3}$ depending on the upper bound $\epsilon_{0}$ );

- (iv) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\lVert\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t})\rVert_{2}<\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}/(4M)$ (by Lemma E.5; the only condition that determines the choice of $T$ );

- (v) $\sigma_{\max}({X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2})\leq c_{4}=2(c_{1}/\kappa_{1})^{1/2}(1+\sqrt{\kappa_{1}})$ .

We are working under $\mu_{\textup{II}}=\mu_{\mathrm{joint}}$ , so $(\hat{\beta}_{\textup{II}}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})$ is sparse. Accordingly, let $S_{\textup{II}}=\mathrm{supp}(\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{stack}})\subset[p]$ . We have the following inequalities:

$$ \displaystyle 0\geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\left[L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t}+\Delta\xi^{t})-L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t})\right] \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\underbrace{\frac{\lambda_{\textup{II}}}{p}\left(\lVert(\xi^{t}+\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}}\rVert_{1}-\lVert(\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}}\rVert_{1}-\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}((\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}})^{{\top}}(\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}}\right)}_{(1)} \displaystyle+\underbrace{\frac{\lambda_{\textup{II}}}{p}\left(\lVert(\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\rVert_{1}-[(s_{\textup{II}}^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}]^{{}^{{\top}}}(\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\right)}_{(2)}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2p}\lVert{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\Delta\xi^{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{(3)}+\frac{1}{p}(\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t}))^{{\top}}\Delta\xi^{t}. $$

The terms $(1)$ , $(2)$ and $(3)$ are all non-negative in the same way that we have asserted so in the proof of Lemma C.6. Then we must have $(\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t}))^{{\top}}\Delta\xi^{t}\leq 0$ . By conditions (i), (iv) of the high-probability event and Cauchy’s inequality, we know

$$ \lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left[(1)+(2)+(3)\leq\frac{1}{p}\lvert(\nabla L_{\textup{II}}(\xi^{t}))^{{\top}}\Delta\xi^{t}\rvert\leq\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}\right]=1. $$

Respectively for terms (2) and (3), the above tells us on the high probability event,

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\rVert_{1}-\frac{1}{p}[(s_{\textup{II}}^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}]^{{}^{{\top}}}(\Delta\xi^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\leq\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}/\lambda_{\textup{II}} \displaystyle 0\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}\Delta\xi^{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}. $$

Take the SVD of ${X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}:\,{X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}\land p}\sigma_{1,i}u_{1,i}v_{1,i}^{{\top}}$ , with $\sigma_{1,1}\geq\sigma_{1,2}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{1,n_{1}\land p}$ . Let $V_{(1)}=\Span(v_{1,i}:\sigma_{1,i}\geq c_{3}/2)$ and $V_{(2)}$ be the orthogonal complement of $V_{(1)}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ . Let $P_{(1)},P_{(2)}$ be the projection matrices onto $V_{(1)}$ and $V_{(2)}$ . Denote $X_{(1)}={X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}P_{(1)}$ and $X_{(1)}={X_{1}^{\mathrm{iid}}}\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}P_{(2)}$ . Then $X_{(1)}^{{\top}}X_{(2)}=0$ . Define $\Delta\xi_{(1)}=P_{(1)}\Delta\xi^{t}$ , $\Delta\xi_{(2)}=P_{(2)}\Delta\xi^{t}$ . The second line of Eqn (E-37) implies

$$ \frac{1}{p}\lVert X_{(1)}\Delta\xi_{(1)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4},\quad\frac{1}{p}\lVert X_{(2)}\Delta\xi_{(2)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}. $$

For $\Delta\xi_{(1)}$ corresponding to the larger singular values, we have

$$ \frac{1}{p}\lVert\Delta\xi_{(1)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 8\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}/(c_{3}^{2})=8\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{2}. $$

We are left to bound $\frac{1}{p}\lVert\Delta\xi_{(2)}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ . We utilize the first line of Eqn (E-37). For $\Delta\xi_{(1)}$ , $\frac{1}{p}[(s_{\textup{II}}^{t})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}]^{{\top}}(\Delta\xi_{(1)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\leq\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(1)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\lVert\Delta\xi_{(1)}\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\epsilon c_{2}c_{3}$ . Since $\Delta\xi_{(2)}=\Delta\xi^{t}-\Delta\xi_{(1)}$ , we know $\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\rVert_{1}-\frac{1}{p}[(s_{\textup{II}}^{t})_{S^{c}}]^{{\top}}(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{c}}\leq\epsilon^{2}\cdot(c_{2}{c_{3}})^{2}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}+4\sqrt{2}\epsilon c_{2}c_{3}$ . Recall that $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c_{2})$ defined in Lemma E.6 is a subset of $S_{\textup{II}}^{c}$ . By the definition of $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c_{2})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})^{c}}\rVert_{1}-\frac{1}{p}(s^{t}_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})^{c}})^{{\top}}(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})^{c}}\leq\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{4}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}+4\sqrt{2}\epsilon c_{2}c_{3} \displaystyle\implies\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})^{c}}\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1}{c_{2}}\left(\epsilon^{2}\cdot c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{2}/\lambda_{\textup{II}}+4\sqrt{2}\epsilon c_{2}c_{3}\right)\leq(\lambda_{\textup{II}}^{-1}+4\sqrt{2})\epsilon c_{3}. $$

Recall we have chosen $\kappa_{1}\,(\overline{\gamma}_{1}+2{\epsilon})\leq\kappa_{1}\,(\overline{\gamma}_{1}+2\epsilon_{0})<1$ as required by Lemma E.13 used for condition (iii) of the high-probability event. Condition (ii) guarantees $\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\rvert\leq p(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+{\epsilon})$ . Then we immediately know $\lvert S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c_{2})^{c}\rvert>p{\epsilon}$ , because otherwise $p=\lvert S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c_{2})^{c}\rvert+\lvert S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\rvert\leq p(\overline{\gamma}_{\textup{II}}+2{\epsilon})<p$ would give a contradiction. We partition $S^{t}_{\textup{II}}(c_{2})^{c}$ disjointly into $S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})^{c}=\cup_{l=1}^{K}S_{l}$ , with each $S_{l}$ satisfying $\lvert S_{l}\rvert\in[p{\epsilon}/2,p{\epsilon}]$ , and they are constructed in a descending order in the sense that for any $i\in S_{l}$ and $j\in S_{l+1}$ , $\lvert({\Delta}\xi_{(2)})_{i}\rvert\geq\lvert(\Delta\hat{\beta}_{(2)})_{j}\rvert$ . By the disjoint partition,

$$ \frac{1}{p}\left\lVert\Delta\xi_{(2)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{p}\left\lVert\left(\Delta\xi_{(2)}\right)_{\cup_{l=2}^{K}S_{l}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\left\lVert\left(\Delta\xi_{(2)}\right)_{S^{t}(c_{2})\cup S_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. $$

We bound the two terms on the RHS respectively. For the first term, same as Eqn (C-26), we eventually get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\left\lVert\left(\Delta\xi_{(2)}\right)_{\cup_{l=2}^{K}S_{l}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4\epsilon c_{3}^{2}(\lambda^{-1}_{\textup{II}}+4\sqrt{2})^{2}. $$

For the second term, we apply conditions (iii), (v) of the high-probability event same as the steps in the proof of Lemma C.6 to get:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\cup S_{1}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{2p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\cup S_{1}}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2c_{4}^{2}}{c_{3}^{2}}\right)\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{\cup_{l=2}^{K}S_{l}}\rVert_{2}^{2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\left(1+\frac{4c_{4}^{2}}{c_{3}^{2}}\right)\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{\cup_{l=2}^{K}S_{l}}\rVert_{2}^{2}. $$

Further, we plug in the bound from Eqn (E-39),

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{S_{\textup{II}}^{t}(c_{2})\cup S_{1}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq \displaystyle\left(1+\frac{4c_{4}^{2}}{c_{3}^{2}}\right)\frac{1}{p}\lVert(\Delta\xi_{(2)})_{\cup_{l=2}^{K}S_{l}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4\epsilon\left(c_{3}^{2}+4c_{4}^{2}\right)(\lambda_{\textup{II}}^{-1}+4\sqrt{2})^{2}, $$

which, put together with Eqn (E-39) and Eqn (E-38), yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert\Delta\xi_{(2)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 8\epsilon\left(c_{3}^{2}+2c_{4}^{2}\right)(\lambda_{\textup{II}}^{-1}+4\sqrt{2})^{2} \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\lVert\Delta\xi^{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left[{8}\epsilon c_{2}^{2}{c_{3}^{2}}+8\left(c_{3}^{2}+2c_{4}^{2}\right)(\lambda_{\textup{II}}^{-1}+4\sqrt{2})^{2}\right]\cdot{\epsilon}\leq\left[{8}+8\left(1+2c_{4}^{2}\right)(\lambda_{\textup{II}}^{-1}+4\sqrt{2})^{2}\right]\cdot{\epsilon}. $$

Recall that $c_{4}=2(c_{1}/\kappa_{1})^{1/2}(1+\sqrt{\kappa_{1}})$ is a fixed constant free of $\epsilon$ .

To re-iterate what we have proved: There exists some small $\epsilon_{0}\in(0,1)$ , s.t. $\forall\,\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0})$ , $\exists\,T$ s.t. $\forall\,t\geq T$ , $\lim_{p}\mathbb{P}\left[\frac{1}{p}\lVert\xi^{t}-\hat{\beta}_{\textup{II}}\rVert_{2}^{2}<\epsilon\right]=1$ . This completes the proof of Lemma E.7. ∎

## Appendix F Supporting Technical Lemmas

#### Lemma F.1 (Relationships Between Pseudo-Lipschitz Functions).

Let $q$ be a fixed known constant. Suppose we have $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}$ that is pseudo-Lipschitz of order $k$ for some $k\geq 1$ , according to Definition 1(a). Define a family of functions $\{\psi_{N}:N=1,2,\cdots\}$ by

$$ \psi_{N}:(\mathbb{R}^{N})^{q}\to\mathbb{R};\quad\psi_{N}(x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in[N]}\psi\left((x_{1})_{j},(x_{2})_{j},\cdots,(x_{q})_{j}\right). $$

Then, $\{\psi_{N}\}$ is uniformly pseudo-Lipschitz iff $1\leq k\leq 2$ ; when it is, it is uniformly pseudo-Lipschitz of order $k$ .

#### Proof of Lemma F.1.

When $k\leq 2$ , we prove $\{\psi_{N}\}$ constructed in such a way must be pseudo-Lipschitz. Since we have argued Defintions 1(a) and 1(b) are compatible, we can write $X=[x_{1}|x_{2}|\cdots|x_{q}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}$ and $Y=[y_{1}|y_{2}|\cdots|y_{q}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}$ , slightly abuse notation by letting $\psi_{N}$ be $\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}\to\mathbb{R}$ and verify Definition 1(b). Then

$$ \displaystyle\lvert\psi_{N}(X)-\psi_{N}(Y)\rvert\leq \displaystyle\frac{L}{N}\sum_{j\in[N]}\left({1+\lVert X_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}+\lVert Y_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}}\right)\cdot\left\lVert X_{j,\cdot}-Y_{j,\cdot}\right\rVert_{2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle L\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in[N]}\left({1+\lVert X_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}+\lVert Y_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}\cdot\frac{\left\lVert X-Y\right\rVert_{F}}{\sqrt{N}}\quad\text{(Cauchy's inequality)}. $$

By the relationship between the spectral norm and the Frobenius norm, $\left\lVert X-Y\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{q}\cdot\left\lVert X-Y\right\rVert_{2}$ . For the sum of squares in the above inequality, we know

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in[N]}\left({1+\lVert X_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}+\lVert Y_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{k-1}}\right)^{2}\leq \displaystyle\frac{3}{N}\sum_{j\in[N]}\left[1+(\lVert X_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{2})^{k-1}+(\lVert Y_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{2})^{k-1}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 3+\frac{3\sum_{j\in[N]}(\lVert X_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{2})^{k-1}}{N}+\frac{3\sum_{j\in[N]}(\lVert Y_{j,\cdot}\rVert_{2}^{2})^{k-1}}{N} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 3+3\left(\frac{\lVert X\rVert_{F}^{2}}{N}\right)^{k-1}+3\left(\frac{\lVert Y\rVert_{F}^{2}}{N}\right)^{k-1}\quad\text{(Jensen's inequality)} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 3q^{k-1}\left[1+\left(\frac{\lVert X\rVert_{2}^{2}}{N}\right)^{k-1}+\left(\frac{\lVert Y\rVert_{2}^{2}}{N}\right)^{k-1}\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 3q^{k-1}\left[1+\left(\frac{\lVert X\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{k-1}+\left(\frac{\lVert Y\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{k-1}\right]^{2}. $$

Plug this into the inequality we have had for $\lvert\psi_{N}(X)-\psi_{N}(Y)\rvert$ , and then we have proved

$$ \lvert\psi_{N}(X)-\psi_{N}(Y)\rvert\leq L\sqrt{3q^{k-1}}\left[1+\left(\frac{\lVert X\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{k-1}+\left(\frac{\lVert Y\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{k-1}\right]\frac{\lVert X-Y\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}, $$

meaning $\{\phi_{N}\}$ is uniformly pseudo-Lipschitz.

When $k>2$ , as long as there is some $\psi$ exactly attaining the rate of the order- $k$ pseudo-Lipschitz bound, we can give a counter-example against $\{\psi_{N}\}$ being uniformly pseudo-Lipschitz. For example, let $q=1$ and $\psi(x)=[(x)_{+}]^{k}$ . We can evaluate the functions at $x=[N,0,0,\cdots,0]^{{\top}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ and $y=\vec{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ . We will notice that as $N\to\infty$ , no finite $L$ can meet the requirement for uniform pseudo-Lipschitz-ness. ∎

#### Lemma F.2.

Let $\Sigma\succcurlyeq 0$ be a covariance matrix, $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}$ and $Z^{{\top}}$ has column vectors drawn iid from $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ . For any order- $k$ uniformly pseudo-Lipschitz functions $\{\phi_{N}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}\to\mathbb{R}\}$ according to Definition 1(b), $\phi_{N}(Z)=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{N}(Z)]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1)$ as $N\to\infty$ .

#### Proof of Lemma F.2.

Without loss of generality, assume $\Sigma$ is invertible. Otherwise, some dimension from $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ can be written as a linear combination of the others, and we can just cut the dimension down from $q$ by only using the other dimensions to eliminate the degeneracy.

We use induction on $q$ . For $q=1$ , it is proved in Lemma 23, Berthier et al. [41]. Now suppose we have proved the results for $q=q_{0}$ and are considering $(q_{0}+1)$ . Equivalently, let’s write $Z=[Z_{1}|Z_{2}]$ where $Z_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q_{0}}$ , $Z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , and each row of $Z=[Z_{1}|Z_{2}]$ is an iid draw from $\mathcal{N}(0,\overline{\Sigma})$ , where

$$ \overline{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}\Sigma&\alpha\\
\alpha^{\top}&\beta.\end{bmatrix} $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{N}(Z_{1},Z_{2})|_{Z_{1}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}} \displaystyle\phi_{N}(Z_{1},\sqrt{\beta-\alpha^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha}\tilde{Z}_{2}+Z_{1}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{Z}_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{N})}\left[\phi_{N}(Z_{1},\sqrt{\beta-\alpha^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha}\tilde{Z}_{2}+Z_{1}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha)\right]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1). $$

Then, using the induction hypothesis,

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{N}(Z_{1},Z_{2})= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{Z_{1}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\tilde{Z}_{2}}}\left[\phi_{N}(Z_{1},\sqrt{\beta-\alpha^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha}\tilde{Z}_{2}+Z_{1}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha)\right]+o_{\mathsf{P}}(1). $$

In the argument, each row of $Z_{1},(\sqrt{\beta-\alpha^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha}\tilde{Z}_{2}+Z_{1}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha)$ is an iid draw from $\mathcal{N}(0,\overline{\Sigma})$ . ∎

#### Lemma F.3 (Extended Stein’s Lemma).

Suppose we have a matrix of jointly normal elements, $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(m_{1}+m_{2})}$ , with two blocks $Z=[Z_{1}|Z_{2}]$ , $Z_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m_{1}}$ and $Z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m_{2}}$ . There is some covariance matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{(m_{1}+m_{2})\times(m_{1}+m_{2})}$ , s.t. $Z^{{\top}}$ has iid column vectors drawn from the $(m_{1}+m_{2})$ -dimensional normal distribution, $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ . In particular, on the same row, the row vectors of $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ have a covariance matrix, $\Sigma_{1,2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}\times m_{2}}$ .

Suppose we have a Lipschitz function $f:\mathbb{R}^{N\times m_{2}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times q}$ , $f^{{\top}}=[f_{1}|f_{2}|\cdots|f_{N}]$ , where $\forall\,j\in[N]$ , $f_{j}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times m_{2}}\to\mathbb{R}^{q}$ is also Lipschitz, with a Jacobian matrix taken only w.r.t. its $j$ -th row denoted as $\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{j,\cdot}}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m_{2}}$ .

Then we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[f(Z_{2})^{{\top}}Z_{1}\right]=\sum_{j\in[N]}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{j,\cdot}}(Z_{2})\right]\Sigma_{1,2}^{{\top}}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m_{1}}. $$

The proof is straightforward and thus omitted. In the proof, it is useful to condition on all other rows when studying one specific row of both $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ .

#### Lemma F.4 (Singular Values of Gaussian Matrices).

Let $\sigma_{\min}(\cdot)$ and $\sigma_{\max}(\cdot)$ denote the smallest and largest non-zero singular values of a matrix. Suppose $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ , $X_{i,j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{N})$ . Consider the asymptotic regime where $N,p\to\infty$ and $\kappa=\lim_{N,p\to\infty}\frac{p}{N}\in(0,\infty)$ . Then we have the following two facts:

- (a) $\lim_{p}\sigma_{\max}(X)=1+\sqrt{\kappa},a.s.,\quad\lim_{p}\sigma_{\min}(X)=\lvert 1-\sqrt{\kappa}\rvert,a.s.$

- (b) There exists $p_{0}$ s.t. $\forall\,p\geq p_{0}$ , $\mathbb{P}\left[\lvert 1-\sqrt{\kappa}\rvert-\epsilon\leq\sigma_{\min}(X)\leq\sigma_{\max}(X)\leq 1+\sqrt{\kappa}+\epsilon\right]\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon^{2}p}{8\kappa}\right).$

Lemma F.4(a) is cited from Theorem 2 of Bai and Yin [82]. Lemma F.4(b) is cited from Corollary 5.35 of Vershynin [83], slightly adapted by re-writing the bound in terms of $\kappa=\lim_{p}p/N$ .

#### Lemma F.5 (Kashin’s Theorem, 1977).

For any positive number $v$ there exist a universal constant $c_{v}$ such that for any $n\geq 1$ , with probability at least $1-2^{-n}$ , for a uniformly random subspace $V_{n,v}$ of dimension $\lfloor n(1-v)\rfloor$ , $\forall x\in V_{n,v}:c_{v}\|x\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|x\|_{1}$ .

#### Lemma F.6 (Non-Asymptotic Singular Value Bounds).

Let $\sigma_{\min}(\cdot)$ and $\sigma_{\max}(\cdot)$ denote the smallest and largest non-zero singular values of a matrix. Suppose $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ , $\{X_{i,j}\}$ are iid Gaussian with the same variance for all $i\in[N],j\in[p]$ . Let $\{\Sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}:i\in[N]\}$ be a collection of covariance matrices satisfying $\min_{i\in[N]}\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{i})>0$ . Let $X_{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ be defined such that $(x_{\Sigma})^{(i)}=x^{(i)}\Sigma_{i}^{1/2}$ , where $(x_{\Sigma})^{(i)},x^{(i)}$ are respectively the $i$ -th rows of $X_{\Sigma}$ and $X$ . Then:

- (a) There exists $\widetilde{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ , s.t. $\widetilde{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}X$ and $\sigma_{\min}(X_{\Sigma})\geq({\min_{i\in[N]}\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{i})})^{1/2}\sigma_{\min}({\widetilde{X}})$ ;

- (b) There exists $\widetilde{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ , s.t. $\widetilde{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}X$ and $\sigma_{\max}(X_{\Sigma})\leq({\max_{i\in[N]}\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_{i})})^{1/2}\sigma_{\max}({\widetilde{X}})$ .

#### Proof of Lemma F.6.

Without loss of generality we let $\mathop{\mathrm{var}}(X_{i,j})=1$ . Let $z_{1},\cdots,z_{N}\in\mathbb{R}$ be iid standard normal variables to be used later. For any $\Sigma_{i},i\in[N]$ , let its spectral decomposition be $\Sigma_{i}=S^{T}_{i}\Lambda_{i}S_{i}$ , where $S$ is orthogonal and $\Lambda_{i}$ is diagonal.

We prove (a) of Lemma F.6, and (b) can be proved analogously. Let $c:=\min_{i\in[N]}\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{i})>0$ . For any vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert X^{\Sigma}v\rVert_{2}^{2}= \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[N]}(x^{(i)}\Sigma_{i}^{1/2}v)^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i\in[N]}(X_{i,\cdot}\Lambda_{i}^{1/2}S_{i}v)^{2}=\sum_{i\in[N]}\left[\sum_{j\in[p]}X_{i,j}\Lambda^{1/2}_{i,j}(S_{i}v)_{j}\right]^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i\in[N]}z^{2}_{i}\cdot\left[\sum_{j\in[p]}\Lambda_{i,j}(S_{i}v)_{j}^{2}\right] \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle c\cdot\sum_{i\in[N]}z_{i}^{2}\cdot\left[\sum_{j\in[p]}(S_{i}v)_{j}^{2}\right]=c\cdot\sum_{i\in[N]}z^{2}_{i}\cdot\lVert v\rVert_{2}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}c\cdot\sum_{i\in[N]}\left[\sum_{j\in[p]}\widetilde{X}_{i,j}v_{j}\right]^{2}=c\cdot\sum_{i\in[N]}\left(\tilde{x}^{(i)}v\right)^{2}=c\,\lVert\widetilde{X}v\rVert_{2}^{2}. $$

As a direct corollary, we know $\|\widetilde{X}v\|_{2}=0$ whenever $\|X^{\Sigma}v\|_{2}=0$ , which means the null space of $X^{\Sigma}$ and $\widetilde{X}$ coincide. Thus the bound holds for smallest non-zero singular value, and we have proved Lemma F.6 (a). ∎
